checks: The two convex hulls with the section as common base lie in K on opposite sides of its plane. For levels in the projection interval their perpendicular heights add to 1/∥u∥. The cone formula applies also when one cone has zero height or when the section has zero area. Dividing the total volume bound by |K| and using coarea gives the pointwise bound p≤d. Outside the projection interval the section is empty. Every threshold displacement a≥0 adds mass at most da, including displacements across either endpoint.

A full-dimensional convex body has positive section area at every interior projection level. Brunn–Minkowski in dimension d−1 makes p^(1/(d−1)) concave there, so log p is finite and concave. The mean lies strictly inside because the law is nondegenerate and supported on the closed interval.

The unweighted Jensen step uses Lebesgue probability measure on the interval of length one and the convex extension s log s with 0 log 0=0. Since ∫p=1, it gives ∫p log p≥0. Bounded p makes p log p integrable. The separate supporting-line step uses the probability p(t)dt. A finite supergradient exists at the interior mean, and the affine term in t−m integrates to zero. Hence log p(m)≥∫p log p≥0.

The bounded concave section root has a finite nonnegative endpoint limit. Interpolation between the mean and the left endpoint limit gives p(m−s)≥p(m)(1−s/A)^(d−1). Its integral is p(m)A[1−(1−a/A)^d]/d. The elementary inequality (1−r)^d≤1−r for 0≤r≤1 gives a/d, also at a=0 and, by monotone convergence, at a=A.

The full-mass centroid result supplies γ_d for the upper cap at m. The hypothesis y∈K places its nonnegative displacement in [0,A]. The cap at ℓ(y) adds exactly that slab up to the null hyperplane at m.
